bio.text: in the flower of his youth he brought the elegance of his brushwork, portraiture, and likeness to such a degree that, if [Mani] and Behzad were living today, they would praise his hand and brush a hundred times a day. In this age he has no rival
bio.lead: Qadi Ahmad, a Safavid chronicler, in the first draft (1596) of his treatise on calligraphers and painters:

source.author: Qadi Ahmad
source.title: Calligraphers and Painters (Gulistan-i hunar)
source.publisher: translated by V. Minorsky, Freer Gallery of Art Occasional Papers (Internet Archive scan)

bio.text: His son, Aga Reza, was a skilled portrait painter, but it is well known that, in recent times, he stupidly abandoned this art in which he had so much skill and took up wrestling, forsaking his talented artist friends. Fortunately, he has now given up this nonsense, but he does not do much painting.

source.author: Eskandar Beg Monshi
source.title: History of Shah ‘Abbas the Great (Tārīk-e ‘Ālamārā-ye ‘Abbāsī)

bio.text: His personality dominates the first half of the century, no doubt partly because it corresponds so clearly to the spirit of the age, democratic, confident, delighting in display and bright colours but conservative in its respect for age and its salute to beauty.

source.author: Basil Gray
source.title: The Arts in the Safavid Period, in The Cambridge History of Iran, vol. 6
